title: Systematic Method: Control of Data and Evidence
abstract: Dewey examines how scientific method achieves rigor not by abandoning the basic inferential structure of ordinary thinking but by systematically controlling the selection, observation, and interpretation of data — transforming raw experience into genuine evidence through hypothesis-guided inquiry.
overview: Chapter Eleven opens Part Two's extended treatment of logic by showing that science does not introduce a new kind of thinking but disciplines the ordinary cycle of inference and testing. Dewey argues that facts do not speak for themselves: only a guiding hypothesis turns observation into purposive data-collection, and only experimental variation isolates which features are causally relevant. The chapter traces the mutual dependence of hypothesis and fact — each constrains and refines the other through successive cycles of observation and inference — and warns that both premature closure on a favored hypothesis and the naive accumulation of unguided observations are characteristic failures of undisciplined thought.

callouts.quote: Reflection is an operation in which facts on one side and meaning on the other are elicited through constant interaction.
callouts.insight: Dewey's framing dissolves the supposed opposition between induction (fact-gathering) and deduction (meaning-application). In genuine inquiry the two poles exist only in and through each other: facts without hypotheses are mute; hypotheses without facts are empty.

callouts.quote: Facts do not select themselves; the mind selects them, and selection is controlled by the dominant interest at the time.
callouts.insight: This claim carries epistemological weight that is still underappreciated: the observer's guiding interest determines what counts as a fact in the first place. The implication for pedagogy is that teaching observation without teaching the habit of posing guiding questions produces not rigorous data-collection but merely passive looking.

callouts.definition: A raw fact is any observed datum; evidence is a fact that has been selected and interpreted as bearing on a specific hypothesis. The transformation from fact to evidence requires a controlling question that makes the observation purposive.
callouts.why_it_matters: This distinction explains why naive empiricism — simply accumulating observations — cannot produce scientific knowledge. Evidence is constituted by the hypothesis it bears upon, which means that inquiry must begin with a provisional interpretive framework.
callouts.modern_echo: Philosophy of science's concept of theory-ladenness of observation directly echoes Dewey's point: what counts as a relevant datum is always relative to an investigative framework.

callouts.definition: The practice of directing perceptual attention by means of a tentative interpretive idea, so that what is noticed and recorded is controlled by the inferential question under investigation rather than by salience or habit.
callouts.why_it_matters: Hypothesis-guided observation is what separates investigation from mere looking. Without it, learners cannot develop the disciplined selectivity that characterizes expert inquiry.
callouts.modern_echo: Contemporary inquiry-based science education emphasizes student-generated research questions precisely to install this hypothesis-first orientation.

callouts.definition: The systematic alteration of one factor while holding others constant, in order to isolate which element of a situation is causally responsible for an observed outcome.
callouts.why_it_matters: Variation is the logical engine of controlled inquiry: it converts correlation into warranted causal inference by eliminating alternative explanations one by one.
callouts.modern_echo: The modern randomized controlled trial is the institutional realization of Dewey's principle of experimental variation, applied at scale with statistical controls.

callouts.misconception: Scientific method is essentially induction — accumulating a sufficient quantity of similar instances until a general law becomes evident.
callouts.correction: Dewey argues that quantity of instances matters far less than quality of contrast. A single well-designed experiment that varies the critical factor and holds others constant yields more causal knowledge than a hundred passive observations of the same unvaried phenomenon.
callouts.still_relevant: Science curricula that emphasize data-collection without teaching hypothesis-formation and experimental design produce students who can observe but not investigate.

callouts.principle: Teach students to formulate a guiding question before any observation activity, and to state what difference in outcome would confirm or disconfirm their tentative answer.
callouts.in_practice: Before a science lab, require students to write: 'I expect X because of Y; if Z happens instead, my hypothesis is wrong.' This pre-commitment forces hypothesis-formation and makes the subsequent observation genuinely purposive rather than passive.

callouts.central_argument: Scientific rigor consists not in abandoning ordinary inferential thinking but in systematically controlling both poles of the inference cycle — hypothesis and observation — so that each disciplines the other through successive rounds of purposive data-collection and conceptual revision.
logical_progression: Ordinary inference leaps from present data to an absent conclusion; science disciplines this leap by requiring explicit statement of the guiding hypothesis before observation begins.
Facts become evidence only when selected and interpreted relative to a hypothesis; hypothesis becomes knowledge only when constrained by evidence gathered under controlled conditions.

Experimental variation — systematically altering one factor while holding others constant — is the technical instrument by which the mutual constraint of hypothesis and evidence achieves the precision that distinguishes scientific from commonsense inquiry.
callouts.bridge_to_next: Having examined how data and evidence are controlled, Chapter Twelve turns to the parallel problem of controlling reasoning itself — the conceptual side of inquiry — through the systematic use of definitions, general principles, and theoretical frameworks.

concepts.name: Evidence
concepts.definition: A fact that has been selected and interpreted as bearing on a specific hypothesis; distinguished from raw data by the controlling question that makes the observation purposive.

concepts.name: Hypothesis-Guided Observation
concepts.definition: Perceptual attention directed by a tentative interpretive idea, making what is noticed and recorded controlled by the investigative question rather than by salience or habit.

concepts.name: Experimental Variation
concepts.definition: Systematic alteration of one factor while holding others constant, isolating which element of a situation is causally responsible for an observed outcome.

concepts.name: Mutual Constraint of Hypothesis and Fact
concepts.definition: The iterative relationship in which hypothesis guides observation and observation revises hypothesis, with each cycle tightening the fit between interpretive idea and empirical datum.

concepts.name: Purposive Data-Collection
concepts.definition: The selection and recording of observations governed by an explicit investigative question, as opposed to passive accumulation of whatever is sensorially salient.

builds_on.reason: Chapter Ten established how concepts become stable through definition and intension/extension; Chapter Eleven shows how those stable concepts function as the hypotheses that direct evidential inquiry.

anticipates.reason: Having treated the control of data through hypothesis-guided observation, Dewey turns in Chapter Twelve to the complementary problem of controlling reasoning through systematic use of concepts and general principles.

contrasts_with.reason: Dewey rejects the view that science proceeds by accumulating instances until patterns become evident; purposive hypothesis-formation precedes and directs observation.
Dewey equally rejects the view that inquiry proceeds from fixed axioms by logical necessity alone; hypotheses must be tested against evidence gathered under controlled conditions.
